title: Shock and hypotension
definition: Shock in canine babesiosis is circulatory failure with poor tissue perfusion: arterial hypotension, clinical collapse, or both, often with hyperlactataemia [R1][R2][R3]. It is mainly a vasodilatory (hyperdynamic) shock on a background of anaemia, seen in complicated B. rossi and B. canis infection [R2][R4].
definition_note: Working definition confirmed, with changes. No study uses the same blood pressure cut-off; each set its own [R1][R5]. Collapse at presentation is the practical marker with outcome data [R3][R6]. Severely anaemic dogs can be tachycardic but normotensive [R7], so anaemia alone is not shock. Reviews name a peracute form, but no study reports it as a separate group [R2]. Hypotension that does not respond to fluid, with organ failure, is reported as 'septic shock' in babesiosis [R8]; the inflammatory response as a whole is on SY11.
key_points: Hypotension is the most frequent blood pressure change in babesiosis and rises with severity: 5 of 10 complicated B. rossi cases, 2 of 10 severe uncomplicated and 0 of 10 mild cases [R1].
Collapse at presentation is the strongest bedside sign: 72 of 320 B. rossi dogs could not stand, and they made up 24 of the 34 deaths [R3].
Measure lactate on arrival and again at 8 and 16 h: in B. rossi, admission lactate above 5 mmol/L, or lactate that stays above 2.5 mmol/L or does not fall by half, was linked with death [R9].
No fluid, vasopressor or steroid has been compared with standard care in dogs with babesiosis; the doses on this page come from general canine critical care [R10].

Give fluid in small boluses and reassess after each: fluid boluses raised mortality in African children with severe febrile illness (57% with malaria) [R11], and liberal fluid caused lung oedema in adults with severe malaria [R12].
Hypotension that does not respond to fluid was fatal in all 10 dogs with babesiosis that had it in one Croatian clinic [R8].

description.heading: What it is
description.text: Dogs with severe and complicated babesiosis often arrive collapsed and in clinical shock [R2][R13]. Arterial pressures fall as severity rises, in B. rossi [R1] and in B. canis [R4][R5]. A low pulse pressure was found in 7 of 10 complicated B. rossi cases [R1]. Reviews compare the shock with the hyperdynamic phase of septic shock [R2]. Severe anaemia adds a lack of oxygen-carrying capacity: B. rossi dogs with a haematocrit of 0.10 to 0.20 L/L (10 to 20%) had a normotensive tachycardia before transfusion [R7].

description.heading: How common, and in which dogs
description.text: At Onderstepoort, 72 of 320 dogs with B. rossi (22.5%) could not stand at presentation [R3], and 21 of 100 dogs had a clinically compromised circulation [R6]. In B. canis, a mean arterial pressure (MAP) below 80 mmHg was found in 7 of 48 dogs in Poland [R5], and a systolic pressure below 100 mmHg in 3 of 49 dogs in Germany [R14]. In a Croatian clinic, 10 of 86 admitted dogs met the authors' criteria for septic shock with refractory hypotension [R8].

description.heading: When in the course of disease
description.text: Shock is present on arrival: in these studies, pressure and lactate were measured before any treatment [R1][R3]. In one Onderstepoort database, 8 of 20 deaths occurred before or at admission, and the treated dogs that died did so within 24 h [R3]. Dogs with refractory hypotension died 1 to 4 days after admission [R8].

description.heading: Mechanism
description.text: A review proposes vasodilation, fluid loss through leaky vessels, dehydration and myocardial depression [R2]. In B. canis, serum TNF-alpha correlated inversely with arterial pressure [R15], and aldosterone rose in some hypotensive dogs, a response the authors judged insufficient [R16]. Hyperlactataemia went with collapse and hypoglycaemia [R17]. In adults with severe malaria, lactic acidosis followed parasite sequestration in small vessels, not low blood volume, and fluid did not correct it [R12]. A Ukrainian group reported a low circulating blood volume by dye dilution, in dogs whose Babesia species was not identified [R18].

species_notes.note: Most of the data. Hypotension rises with severity [R1]; collapse and lactate predict death [R3][R9]. Adrenal insufficiency was not found [R19].

Complicated cases had lower pressures than uncomplicated cases (MAP 60 versus 116 mmHg, abstract values) [R4]. Hypotension went with azotaemia [R5]. All 8 non-survivors of 15 dogs had hyperlactataemia [R20].

The Ukrainian shock and infusion studies [R18][R21], the Croatian septic shock series (species not stated in the abstract) [R8] and the Indian echocardiography series [R22] did not name the species. No blood pressure data were found for B. gibsoni or B. vogeli.

criteria.threshold: More than 3 SD below the mean of healthy controls (controls: systolic 151 ± 11 mmHg, MAP 107 ± 10 mmHg)
criteria.note: 30 dogs with B. rossi and 10 healthy controls, South Africa. Method not given in the abstract.
48 dogs with B. canis, Poland, measured at the first visit before treatment.
49 dogs with B. canis, Germany; median systolic 119 mmHg (range 90 to 180).

criteria.threshold: Unable to stand unaided at presentation
criteria.note: 320 dogs with B. rossi. The marker with the strongest outcome data.
B. rossi. The source of the 2.5 mmol/L cut-off gave it as 22.5 mg per 100 mL.

criteria.criterion: Septic shock (consensus, dogs with sepsis from any cause)
criteria.threshold: Impaired perfusion despite adequate fluid resuscitation: hyperlactataemia, persistent hypotension, progressive organ dysfunction
criteria.note: The 2026 consensus gives no numeric cut-off for dogs. Babesiosis is not bacterial sepsis; the label is used for babesiosis by one group [R8].

criteria.threshold: Systolic above 90 mmHg or MAP above 65 mmHg, sustained for at least 4 h
criteria.note: End point of a study of 47 dogs with septic shock; not a guideline target.

criteria.criterion: Shock index (heart rate divided by systolic pressure)
criteria.threshold: No validated cut-off; 1.43 ± 0.3 in dogs with babesiosis and shock versus 0.76 ± 0.2 in healthy dogs
criteria.note: 30 dogs, Ukraine, Babesia species not identified.

clinical_signs.note: 22.5% of 320 B. rossi dogs; odds ratio for death 8.36 [R3].
Lower in collapsed dogs and in dogs that died; odds of death rose 1.39 times for each 1 °C decrease [R3].
Pulse 122 versus 86 beats/min in healthy dogs [R18]; also present in severely anaemic dogs with normal pressure [R7].
Low pulse pressure in 7 of 10 complicated B. rossi cases [R1].
Did not relate to arterial pressure in B. rossi; pale membranes do not show whether the dog is hypotensive [R1].
Proposed with collapse as a simple severity marker for B. rossi [R13]; see SY08 for lung injury.

tests.finding: Low systolic, diastolic and mean pressures in complicated disease [R1][R5].
tests.note: One reading at admission was used in the studies; serial readings are recommended [R4].

tests.finding: Above 2 mmol/L in 55.5% of 209 B. rossi dogs; median 4.3 mmol/L in dogs that died [R3].
tests.note: Repeat at 8 and 16 h; the trend predicts outcome better than one value [R9]. A hand-held analyser was used in B. canis [R20].

tests.finding: Hypoglycaemia (below 3.3 mmol/L) in 19.2% of 317 B. rossi dogs; glucose and lactate correlated inversely [R3].
tests.note: Hypoglycaemia was linked with collapse and hyperlactataemia [R17]. Treatment is on SY16.

tests.finding: Separates anaemic dogs from haemoconcentrated dogs: haematocrit above 0.55 L/L in 4 of 320 B. rossi dogs, 3 of whom died [R3].
tests.note: Haemoconcentration is on SY14; anaemia on SY01.

tests.finding: Pressures correlated inversely with creatinine and urea in B. canis [R5]; creatinine above 106 µmol/L had an odds ratio for death of 7.55 in B. rossi [R3].
tests.note: Acute kidney injury is on SY05.

tests.finding: Mixed metabolic acidosis and respiratory alkalosis in 31 of 34 severe B. rossi cases; 82% were hyperlactataemic [R25].
tests.note: Base excess was negative in all 34 dogs [R25].

tests.finding: Diastolic dysfunction was common in an Indian series and went with higher mortality [R22].

differentials.distinguish: Tachycardia with normal pressure and a haematocrit of 0.10 to 0.20 L/L (10 to 20%) [R7]. Treat the anaemia (SY01).
Collapse or cerebral signs with blood glucose below 3.3 mmol/L [R3]. Measure glucose in every collapsed dog (SY16).
Acute cerebral signs with normal or high glucose; all 6 such dogs died [R3]. See SY07.
Myocardial injury and arrhythmias are reported in babesiosis [R2]; echocardiography shows systolic or diastolic dysfunction [R22]. See SY09.
High haematocrit despite haemolysis; not explained by dehydration [R3]. See SY14.
The Onderstepoort series excluded dogs with B. vogeli, Ehrlichia canis or Theileria by PCR, so their effect on shock is not known [R3].

approach.detail: Note whether the dog can stand, and measure heart rate, pulse, rectal temperature, arterial pressure, lactate, glucose and haematocrit before treatment [R3][R9].
Hypoglycaemia is common in collapsed dogs and raises the odds of death [R3]. Doses are on SY16.
Standard care in the Onderstepoort series included diminazene, transfusion and intravenous fluid [R3]. Drugs and doses are on TX00.

approach.action: Give small crystalloid boluses if perfusion is poor
approach.detail: Balanced isotonic crystalloid, 10 to 15 mL/kg at a time, with reassessment after each bolus [R10]. Avoid liberal volumes: bolus fluid raised mortality in febrile African children [R11] and caused lung oedema in adults with malaria [R12].
In a severely anaemic, tachycardic dog, the missing part is oxygen-carrying capacity. Packed red cells improved acid-base status and pressure in B. rossi [R7]. Transfusion guidance is on SY01.
Lactate that stays above 2.5 mmol/L, or falls by less than half, predicted death in B. rossi [R9].

Hypotension that persists after fluid is an indication for a vasopressor infusion [R10]; the canine consensus defines septic shock as impaired perfusion despite adequate fluid [R23]. Refractory hypotension carried a very high mortality [R8].

approach.action: Watch for lung oedema and kidney injury
approach.detail: Fluid loading can worsen lung oedema [R12], and low pressure went with azotaemia [R5]. See SY08 and SY05.

treatments.name: Isotonic crystalloid bolus
treatments.aim: Restore circulating volume and perfusion in a dog that is hypovolaemic or dehydrated.
treatments.evidence_summary: Intravenous crystalloid is part of standard care in B. rossi [R3] and B. canis (45 of 49 dogs in Germany) [R14], and a review advises it for dehydrated or hypovolaemic dogs [R26]. It was never compared with other fluids or with no bolus in babesiosis. In 3141 African children with severe febrile illness (57% with malaria), boluses of 20 to 40 mL/kg raised 48-hour mortality (relative risk 1.45) [R11]. In 28 adults with severe malaria, liberal saline did not improve acid-base status or kidney function, and 8 developed lung oedema [R12]. Evidence for the dose is a canine sepsis review (level E) [R10].

doses.drug: balanced isotonic crystalloid (for example lactated Ringer's solution)
doses.context: Dogs and cats with sepsis and hypoperfusion, without heart disease; narrative review
doses.note: Not tested in babesiosis. The review prefers balanced solutions to 0.9% saline.

treatments.cautions: Lung oedema is a complication of babesiosis (SY08) and was made worse by fluid loading in malaria [R12]. Fluid boluses increased mortality in African children with severe febrile illness [R11]. Signs of fluid overload include weight gain, serous nasal discharge, rising respiratory rate and effort, and effusions [R10].
treatments.monitoring: Reassess after each bolus for fluid responsiveness, and check fluid needs every 4 to 6 h by examination and body weight [R10]. Lactate at 8 and 16 h [R9].

treatments.name: Packed red cell transfusion
treatments.aim: Restore oxygen-carrying capacity in the anaemic dog in shock.
treatments.evidence_summary: In a randomised trial in 12 dogs with B. rossi and a haematocrit of 0.10 to 0.20 L/L (10 to 20%), packed red cells and a haemoglobin-based oxygen carrier gave similar improvements in blood gas, acid-base status and pressure; dogs given packed cells regained demeanour and appetite faster [R7]. There was no group without transfusion. Transfusion was part of standard care in the Onderstepoort series [R3]. Indications and products are on SY01.

doses.route: IV (central venous catheter in the trial)
doses.context: B. rossi, 12 dogs (8 to 25 kg), randomised trial
doses.note: Followed by lactated Ringer's solution in the trial. See SY01 for transfusion guidance.

treatments.cautions: Central venous oxygen tension stayed below normal in both groups over 72 h, so transfusion did not fully restore tissue oxygenation [R7].
treatments.monitoring: Haematocrit, heart rate, arterial pressure and lactate [R7][R9].

treatments.name: Noradrenaline (norepinephrine) infusion
treatments.aim: Restore vascular tone and arterial pressure when hypotension persists after fluid.
treatments.evidence_summary: No study of noradrenaline in dogs with babesiosis was found. A review of fluid therapy in canine and feline sepsis names noradrenaline as the vasopressor of choice when hypotension persists after fluid, and says early use improved haemodynamics [R10]. The canine sepsis consensus defines septic shock by impaired perfusion despite adequate fluid [R23]. Its use in babesiosis is extrapolated.

doses.context: Dogs and cats with septic shock; narrative review
doses.note: Not tested in babesiosis. Give only after fluid resuscitation.

treatments.cautions: Use only after fluid resuscitation [R10]. In dogs with septic shock, all responded at first to vasopressors, but sustained resolution of hypotension took hours [R24].
treatments.monitoring: Arterial pressure continuously; a septic shock study used systolic above 90 mmHg or MAP above 65 mmHg for 4 h as resolution [R24]. Lactate and urine output.

treatments.name: Dopamine infusion
treatments.aim: Support contractility and pressure in a dog with systolic dysfunction.
treatments.evidence_summary: In an Indian series of 92 dogs with intraerythrocytic parasites and SIRS, sepsis or septic shock, dogs with systolic dysfunction on echocardiography were given dopamine; its effect was not reported separately [R22]. Only 2 dogs had systolic dysfunction alone and 5 had both systolic and diastolic dysfunction [R22]. A canine sepsis review prefers noradrenaline as the vasopressor [R10]. See SY09.

doses.context: Babesia species not identified, India, case series; given for systolic dysfunction
doses.note: Effect not reported. Cardiac use is on SY09.

treatments.cautions: No safety data in babesiosis. Arrhythmias are reported in babesiosis [R2].
treatments.monitoring: The series did not describe monitoring [R22]. Ventricular arrhythmias in babesiosis go with myocardial injury [R2].

treatments.name: Hypertonic saline bolus
treatments.aim: Rapid small-volume expansion of the circulating volume.
treatments.evidence_summary: Not studied in babesiosis. In a randomised trial in 23 dogs with gastric dilatation-volvulus and shock, 7.5% saline was compared with hydroxyethyl starch; both caused a tendency to hypocoagulability on thromboelastometry [R27]. The trial measured haemostasis, not survival.

doses.context: Dogs with gastric dilatation-volvulus and shock, 10 dogs in this arm, randomised trial
doses.note: Abstract only; the number of boluses is not given in the abstract. Not tested in babesiosis.

treatments.cautions: Hypocoagulability after the bolus [R27] matters in babesiosis with coagulopathy (SY03).
treatments.monitoring: The trial measured coagulation times, fibrinogen and thromboelastometry after the bolus [R27].

treatments.name: Dextran 40 (rheopolyglucin), alone or with dipyridamole
treatments.aim: Expand circulating volume and reduce red cell and platelet aggregation.
treatments.evidence_summary: Level A by design only. One Ukrainian group (one cohort published twice) treated dogs with acute babesiosis and shock, species not identified. In 30 dogs, rheopolyglucin restored blood volume and pressure better than a sorbitol-lactate crystalloid, which reduced aggregation better [R18]. In 100 dogs, a dextran-dipyridamole mixture restored the measured values for 48 h and worked better than either drug alone [R21]. End points were laboratory and pressure values; survival was not reported.

doses.drug: rheopolyglucin (10% dextran, molecular weight 30000 to 40000, in 0.9% sodium chloride)
doses.context: Babesia species not identified, 15 dogs per arm, Ukraine, comparison of two infusions
doses.note: The authors advise it in the first hours, then combined with the crystalloid.

doses.context: Babesia species not identified, 15 dogs per arm, Ukraine, comparison of two infusions

doses.drug: rheopolyglucin with dipyridamole, as one infusion mixture
doses.context: Babesia species not identified, 100 dogs, Ukraine, trial
doses.note: Abstract only. The abstract gives 45 mg dextran and 2.5 mg dipyridamole per kg; this does not match 5 mL/kg of a 10% solution. Check the full text before use.

treatments.cautions: No adverse effects were reported [R18]. Dextran is a synthetic colloid; the kidney harm data in dogs are for hydroxyethyl starch, not dextran [R28].
treatments.monitoring: The studies measured arterial pressure, shock index, haematocrit and blood volume at 24, 48 and 72 h [R18].

treatments.name: Hydroxyethyl starch
treatments.aim: Expand circulating volume with a synthetic colloid.
treatments.evidence_summary: In a cohort of 422 dogs in intensive care, 10% hydroxyethyl starch was an independent risk factor for death or acute kidney injury (adjusted odds ratio 1.98; number needed to harm 6) [R28]. A canine sepsis review does not recommend synthetic colloids [R10]. In the Indian babesiosis series, 6% starch at 5 mL/kg/h was given for diastolic dysfunction, with no outcome reported by treatment [R22].
treatments.cautions: Risk of acute kidney injury and death [R28]; kidney injury is already a complication of babesiosis (SY05). Starch caused a tendency to hypocoagulability in dogs with gastric dilatation-volvulus [R27].
treatments.monitoring: The cohort defined kidney injury as a twofold rise in creatinine, or oliguria or anuria for 12 h or more [R28].

treatments.name: Hydrocortisone
treatments.aim: Treat suspected corticosteroid insufficiency in vasopressor-dependent shock.
treatments.evidence_summary: Not tested in babesiosis. In 47 dogs with septic shock, the 21 given hydrocortisone were sicker at baseline, took longer to reach sustained resolution of hypotension (8.5 versus 4 h), and had no better survival (14.3% versus 34.6%, not significant) [R24]. In 68 dogs with B. rossi, the ACTH stimulation test found no adrenal insufficiency; cortisol was highest in dogs that died [R19]. High cortisol also predicted death in 320 B. rossi dogs [R3].
treatments.cautions: No dose is given: the sources read did not state one.

prognosis.text: Shock marks the dogs most likely to die. In 320 B. rossi dogs, collapse at presentation had an odds ratio for death of 8.36; overall 10.6% died (the source did not separate euthanasia) [R3]. A compromised circulation was linked with death in 100 B. rossi dogs [R6]. Arterial pressure itself did not differ between survivors and non-survivors in 30 B. rossi dogs [R1]. All 10 dogs with refractory hypotension and organ failure died, against 2.6% of the other admitted dogs [R8].

indicators.meaning: Odds ratio for death 8.36 in B. rossi; 24 of 34 deaths were in collapsed dogs [R3].
Linked with death in 90 dogs with severe or complicated B. rossi [R9].

indicators.finding: Lactate above 2.5 mmol/L at 8, 16 or 24 h, or a fall of less than 50% in 8 to 16 h
indicators.meaning: Linked with death; lactate persistently above 4.4 mmol/L meant a very poor prognosis [R9].
Separated all 8 non-survivors from 7 survivors in a small Swiss series; 2 of the non-survivors were euthanised [R20].
Dogs with a compromised circulation had higher parasitaemias and were more likely to die [R6].
Odds of death rose 1.39 times for each 1 °C decrease [R3].

related.why: Complicated disease, SIRS and multiple organ dysfunction; triage and order of care.
Hypoglycaemia and lactate as metabolic problems.
Lung oedema, a risk of fluid loading.
Coagulopathy, relevant to colloids and hypertonic saline.

evidence_gaps: No trial has compared fluid types, volumes or end points in dogs with babesiosis.
No vasopressor (noradrenaline, vasopressin) has been tested in babesiosis; no canine dose source for vasopressin was read in this run.
No data were found on oxygen therapy in shocked dogs with babesiosis.
Blood volume has not been measured in B. rossi; the only blood volume data come from dogs whose Babesia species was not identified.
There is no validated blood pressure cut-off for babesiosis, and measurement methods differ between studies.
Whether hyperlactataemia in babesiosis reflects poor perfusion or other causes, as parasite sequestration does in human malaria, is not known.
Hypertonic saline, albumin and corticosteroids have not been studied in babesiosis.
No shock data were found for B. gibsoni or B. vogeli.

search.note: Searched the local review (treatment set, disorder terms, full texts) and PubMed and Europe PMC for canine babesiosis with hypotension, blood pressure, shock, lactate, collapse and each candidate treatment, then canine sepsis fluid and vasopressor sources and human malaria fluid trials. The 2024 AAHA fluid therapy guidelines could not be opened (access blocked) and are not cited. Organ failures after shock are on the organ pages.
